authorities.proposition: A person commits an offence if they behave in a threatening or abusive manner, the behaviour would be likely to cause a reasonable person to suffer fear or alarm, and they intend to cause fear or alarm or are reckless as to whether the behaviour would cause it (s.38(1)). It is a defence to show the behaviour was, in the particular circumstances, reasonable (s.38(2)). The offence applies to a single act or a course of conduct, and to things said/communicated as well as things done (s.38(3), not independently re-fetched this session).
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, on two independent passes, word-for-word consistent both times.

authorities.name: Rooney v Procurator Fiscal, Stirling
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Menzies, Lady Dorrian (delivering the Opinion of the Court), Lord Tyre
authorities.proposition: S.38(1)(b)'s 'likely to cause a reasonable person to suffer fear or alarm' element is wholly objective: it is irrelevant whether the actual complainer was in fact frightened or alarmed. The matter is decided on an objective basis from the standpoint of the reasonable person placed in the complainer's actual situation and context - not by reference to the complainer's individual reaction or personal fortitude. On the facts, the appellant's conviction for shouting sectarian and racist threats of violence at police officers who were not themselves fearful or alarmed was upheld, because a reasonable person in the officers' situation would likely have been caused fear or alarm even though these particular officers were not. Appeal refused.
